speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (a) whether he can provide an update on Phases 1 and 2 of Project Wolbachia in the control of the Aedes aegypti mosquito vector; (b) how long will the Phase 3 field study last; and (c) whether Project Wolbachia can be accelerated in light of the increased incidents of dengue infections in the first quarter of 2019.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (a) what are the causes of the sudden spike of dengue cases in the first quarter of 2019; (b) what are the measures in place to detect dengue cases early; and (c) what is the Ministry's plan to reduce dengue cases, especially during the dengue peak seasons.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Neighbouring countries have also reported increases in dengue cases in recent months.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Contributing to this situation is a persistently high Aedes aegypti mosquito population in the community, as detected by the NEA Gravitrap surveillance system.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As a regional transport hub, Singapore is vulnerable to the transmission of infectious diseases.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA and the Ministry of Health have put in place a robust surveillance system to detect dengue and other vector-borne diseases.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This system comprises vector surveillance, virus surveillance and dengue case surveillance.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA has an island-wide network of 50,000 Gravitraps to monitor the mosquito population and will add another 14,000 Gravitraps in the second half of 2019.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Data from this network guides NEA’s vector control efforts, allowing officers to quickly zero in on the areas with high mosquito population.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA’s laboratory-based virus surveillance system monitors dengue virus serotypes and provides early alerts when there is a serotype switch.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Historically, such switches have preceded large dengue outbreaks.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Further, NEA, together with the National University of Singapore, has developed a model which helps us to forecast dengue incidence.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This allows NEA to coordinate an effective pre-emptive response to impending dengue outbreaks.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA anticipates an increasing trend of dengue cases in the warmer months ahead and has taken concerted efforts to stem dengue transmission.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First, NEA, together with various agencies represented in the Inter-Agency Dengue Task Force, has stepped up checks and conducted more than 224,000 inspections in the months leading up to the peak dengue season.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: About 2,900 instances of mosquito breeding were removed.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Second, NEA brought forward the launch of the 2019 National Dengue Prevention Campaign to 7 April this year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Together with Grassroots Advisers and leaders and Dengue Prevention Volunteers, NEA has been raising awareness that clean and stagnant water in homes are potential breeding habitats for mosquitoes and galvanising the community to step up dengue prevention efforts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: More than 8,500 volunteers have been trained to conduct patrols and house visits to share dengue prevention tips with residents.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Technology and innovation are another key pillar in dengue prevention efforts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA is conducting trial releases of male Wolbachia-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes to further suppress the urban Aedes aegypti mosquito population in the community.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA has successfully completed the Phases 1 and 2 field studies for Project Wolbachia in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: More importantly, this initial phase provided NEA with valuable data on the behaviour of the Wolbachia-Aedes mosquito.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This has helped NEA to design more effective release strategies for Singapore’s high-density and high-rise city environment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In this phase, NEA expanded the size of the study sites and released male Wolbachia-Aedes mosquitoes at higher floors, in addition to releases at the ground floor.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The results showed that a larger release site yielded improved population suppression results.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Phase 3 field study has started in February 2019.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA has further expanded the study sites at Nee Soon East and Tampines West by 1.6 to 2.2 times.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA aims to determine if suppression of the Aedes aegypti mosquito population can be sustained in larger areas and if a smaller number of male Wolbachia-Aedes mosquitoes can be released at each residential block to maintain the suppression.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA is also developing automation for male Wolbachia-Aedes mosquito production and release, to ensure scalability of the technology.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will evaluate the Wolbachia-Aedes technology carefully and rigorously before deploying it on a large scale.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will continue to provide regular updates on the progress of Project Wolbachia.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We continue to see many cases of mosquito breeding in homes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: All it takes is a small amount of water, the size of a 20-cent coin, for mosquitoes to breed.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With a short breeding cycle of seven days, keeping the mosquito population in check requires the joint efforts of every individual and stakeholder in the community to eradicate mosquito breeding habitats by practising good housekeeping and doing the five-step Mozzie Wipeout.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Government alone cannot prevent dengue transmission in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We must remain vigilant and work together to keep dengue at bay.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Compared to many other countries, we seem to be slower in our pace of introduction of Wolbachia as a dengue and Zika suppression method.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My second question is: will NEA consider adopting the World Mosquito Programme's Wolbachia method, which is to release both male and female Wolbachia mosquitoes so that it is self-sustaining?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This has found success in several hotspots internationally, including Australia.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My third question has to do with availability of information on Project Wolbachia as well as educating the public.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It seems that the public is aware of various methods but may not be so clear about the benefits of Wolbachia.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Australia, for example, they involved school students as part of the release of male Wolbachia mosquitoes so that they bring the message home to their families as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, will NEA consider expanding on the education and information available on this project?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, as I have said in my answer earlier, when we did Phase 1, it gave us valuable information on the deployment of the technology, particularly because we are the first in the world to implement this technology in a tropical, highly urbanised and high-density landscape.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: From the information that we got about the behaviour of the male Wolbachia-Aedes aegypti, we were able to then implement Phase 2 in terms of where to launch and deploy these mosquitoes to both higher floors and lower floors, as well as having larger areas and buffer sites to improve the suppression of the Aedes aegypti mosquito population.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And as I have said, we want to carefully and rigorously evaluate the results to see if the suppression can be sustained, before we consider deploying this on a larger scale.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, let me say that, to our knowledge, for countries that have adopted the Wolbachia technology, even though the technology has developed quite quickly, none of them has actually gone beyond field trials into full scale implementation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Australia, I understand, has completed the field trials but they have not expanded the project.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Even in Guangzhou, what they have done is similar to Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They have actually just expanded the field trials.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, source reduction and so on are still important and are, in fact, critical to the success of this Project Wolbachia technology and we will have to continue to persist with such efforts in order to restrict and reduce the number of dengue cases.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Regarding education, let me say that we are working on educating both the residents within the field trial study sites as well as the general public through various means, such as the mass media, by having articles on the Wolbachia technology, community outreach events as well as seminars.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Since 2012, we have organised more than a hundred seminars and outreach events to reach out to academia, the medical and healthcare professionals, teachers, students, non-government organisations, grassroots leaders, members of the public and residents.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We also have the Project Wolbachia Learning Journey which we offer to members of the public, students, residents from the study area, to visit our mosquito production facility, so that they will have a better understanding of the processes involved and the production of our Wolbachia-Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to scaling and sustainability, I think I have more or less touched on that question.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of the private condominiums in my constituency – and I have many – are stepping up anti-mosquito fogging.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It has come to a point where there is some kind of fogging almost every day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The residents tell me, "If I do not fog, then the mosquitoes next door will come over to my side".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Two, because there is so much fogging taking place and it is becoming like a competition, can NEA consider coordinating such fogging activities in private estate clusters where there are quite a number of condominiums and they are all fogging at some point in the week.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And if it is effective, then I think we should do something about it.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In fact, if somebody coordinates, then if we can aggregate demand, it may also bring the costs down for the area or for the estate.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I said earlier in my reply that we have a Gravitrap surveillance system.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It is deployed island-wide and the idea is to identify where there is a high concentration of Aedes aegypti mosquito population.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, fogging is normally used when there is a dengue cluster, because fogging and misting is to kill the adult mosquitoes and also where there could be a high concentration of mosquito population.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But there is a use for fogging and misting, as I have said, during a dengue cluster or when there is a high mosquito population.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: When there is a dengue cluster, you also have indoor space spraying to kill the adult mosquitoes which may be infected.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to fogging becoming a competition amongst condominiums, I think the fogging schedule is determined by the Management Committee of the condominium.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, they need to decide if there is a real need to do fogging so frequently.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: First, I want to thank NEA for allowing Jurong students and parents to visit the Wolbachia production facility in Jurong.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It was very well-received and we were very encouraged by the project.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I have two questions to ask the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: First, since the production facility is in Jurong, is there any plan to extend the Wolbachia project in Jurong as well because there are also dengue clusters?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Two, is there a plan to expand the Wolbachia production facility?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For instance, we work with various companies like Orinno Technology and Verily Life Sciences to develop innovative devices, such as a larvae counter, pupae counter and sorter, adult mosquito sex sorter, mosquito launcher and so on to make it more effective and efficient in producing these Wolbachia-Aedes mosquitoes.
